## Teaching philosophy

<!-- From tex/Leingang_TS.tex in leingang/cv (2024). Relative dates such as
     "three years ago" date from 2024; update as needed. -->

I have recently come to realize that I view my students through the eyes of my
children. When my children were small, I found my students big and
intimidating. Now that the kids are of college age, I find many parallels
between teaching and parenting.

**Curiosity.** I believe in fostering a growth mindset in my students by
modeling it myself. I also seek to instill an appreciation of the beauty of
mathematics.

I adapted my teaching techniques during the remote instruction year of the
COVID-19 pandemic, practices that I continue today. I structure classes around
frequent, repeated practice. Students complete a survey before each class.
There are content questions to gauge understanding, but the most valuable
question is open-ended: "What questions do you have?" Student responses inform
my choices during class.

**Compassion.** I discovered through experience that children are not
"projects" of their parents. Instead, they are unique human beings with their
own thoughts, interests, plans, and dreams. In the same way, I cannot form
every one of my students into a mini-me math major. But I can learn about them
and how to reach them.

I studied Mandarin for four years to better understand my Chinese
students, and how to help them learn to write mathematical proofs in English. I
make a point of learning students' pronouns and name pronunciations. I still
livestream and record class for students who are unable to attend. I have
strived to make my classroom and office a safe space for LGBTQ+ students.

**Commitment.** The word *asymptote* in math describes a line that a curve
approaches but never meets. In my nearly 25 years of teaching, I have spent
close to 5,000 hours in the classroom alone, and twice that preparing and
reflecting. But I feel that perfect teaching, much like perfect parenting, is
an asymptote that can never be reached. The best one can do is commit
everything to the craft, and aim for continuous growth.

## Program leadership at NYU

**Vice Chair for Undergraduate Affairs** (2008–2023), then **Assistant Director
for Undergraduate Studies** (2023–2025), Department of Mathematics:

- Directed the service-level mathematics program, which teaches about 7,000
  students each academic year in calculus, precalculus, discrete mathematics,
  quantitative reasoning, and linear algebra.
- Developed a common syllabus for Calculus I, II, and III and instituted a
  course coordination system to normalize academic content and policies.
- Managed and led a team of 12 clinical faculty, and led clinical faculty
  recruitment each year.
- Directed training for novice teachers: graduate teaching assistants,
  postdoctoral lecturers, and undergraduate tutors and graders.
- Managed student affairs: honors, credit transfers, graduation requirements,
  academic integrity, and other sensitive student issues.
- Managed learning outcomes assessment for service-level courses.

## Preparing teachers

- **Mathematics department teaching seminar**, NYU (2010–2022), developed with
  A. Hanhart, C. Clarkson, and other clinical faculty.
- **Teaching Undergraduate Mathematics Seminar (TUMS)**, Harvard (2005–2008).
  Expanded the Apprentice program into a mandatory pre-service seminar on
  lesson planning, classroom management, and public speaking, and reorganized
  TUMS into an in-service seminar based on case studies.
- **Apprentice coach**, Harvard (2003–2008). Mentored graduate students who
  observed one week of my class, then taught for a week.
- **A.L.M. in Teaching program**, Harvard Extension School (2003–2008).
  Content courses in geometry and probability for middle- and high-school
  teachers.
- **MAA OPEN Math** (2022–), selection committee and advisory board for an
  NSF-funded professional development project.

- **MATH-UA 121 Calculus I** (2014), with S. Kalayçioglu: a hybrid online course

- **MATH-UA 270 Transformations and Geometries** (2012), reformed with

- **MATH-UA 325 Analysis I** (2011), taught in a traditional Moore Method format.

## Broadening participation

**NYU Courant GSTEM** (founded 2012). A six-week summer program that raises
representation in STEM through mentorship and community. Students do
supervised research projects and attend lectures, panels, and field trips.
Close to 400 high school students have taken part. I was principal
investigator on a \$500K grant from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
